strengths: Well-motivated observation that offline SFT performance does not translate to post-RL performance; Figure 1 convincingly demonstrates offline-online ranking reversals
Sound application of off-policy evaluation theory to correct behavior-target policy mismatch, with clear connection to importance sampling
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 6 model families and multiple benchmarks with substantial empirical gains (14.6% Pass@8 on AIME-2025, 40% absolute accuracy on logic games)
Practical method that works as a plug-in reweighting approach with both NLL and KL objectives, applicable to different model sizes
Thorough analysis including gradient alignment (Figure 7), parameter drift (Figure 8), and transfer to different task distributions (Table 4)
Clear presentation of motivation, method variants, and algorithm; Figure 2 provides excellent intuition
weaknesses: Limited novelty: applies well-established OPE techniques to a new problem; concurrent works (iw-SFT, DFT, AwSFT, Proximal-SFT) propose similar importance-weighting schemes but are not experimentally compared, only citing a generic 'Single Step IS' baseline
Scope restricted to verifiable reasoning tasks with deterministic correctness labels; generalizability to open-ended generation, knowledge tasks, or other capabilities is unclear and untested

Critical experimental gaps: Figure 1 lacks error bars/confidence intervals despite RL variance; missing ablations on hyperparameters (γ=0.999, clipping bounds, block size B); no seed averaging reported; unclear if ranking reversals are statistically significant

Incomplete description of design choices: negative example selection (§3.6, §4.5) underdocumented; offline data generated from Qwen3-8B makes it unclear whether improvements come from PEAR or stronger baseline data

Theoretical gaps: no formal analysis of why this reweighting leads to better RL initialization; connection between suffix ratios and Q-values (Appendix C) is intuitive but hand-wavy; offline data generation mechanism (behavior policy specification) may not hold in practice

Methodological concerns: Table 4 shows dramatic performance variation across task distributions (2.8%→38.3% for 1.7B), suggesting potential fragility; analysis findings somewhat tautological (RQ1) or modest (RQ2 gradient angle 51.27°→52.53°); causality between NSS and RL performance unclear
Missing comparisons to closely related concurrent work despite citing 6+ similar methods; no evaluation on other RL algorithms beyond GRPO or other capability domains

strengths: Important practical observation that offline SFT performance does not reliably predict post-RL performance, demonstrated convincingly in Figure 1
Principled approach using importance weighting grounded in off-policy evaluation theory (Precup et al. 2000)
Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning synthetic reasoning games and mathematical benchmarks across 6 models of varying sizes
Multiple method variants (sequence-level, token-level, block-level) offering flexibility and exploring stability-granularity tradeoffs
Useful analytical insights in Section 4.6 examining what positions PEAR concentrates learning on and how it affects gradient alignment with online RL
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty—straightforward application of well-established OPE techniques to SFT without significant innovation; concurrent work (Wu et al. 2025, Zhang et al. 2025a, Zhu et al. 2025d) proposes related ideas
Missing experimental comparisons with concurrent methods (DFT, iw-SFT, ASFT, Proximal-SFT); only compares to authors' own strawman baseline (Single Step IS)

Heterogeneous and insufficiently validated results: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; results appear to be single runs; improvements vary dramatically across models (DS-Qwen +50pp vs. Qwen3-8B +4pp) with no explanation

Weak conceptual justification: why this specific behavior-target mismatch is the binding constraint, and why importance weighting (high variance over long sequences) is preferable to alternatives, is not convincingly argued

Hyperparameter sensitivity unexplored: γ=0.999, log-ratio clip bounds [-0.08, 0.3], and block size B are set but lack ablations or sensitivity analysis, making practical implementation guidance unclear
Insufficient discussion of π_β specification: PEAR requires accurate data-generating policy specification, but robustness to π_β misspecification and practical guidance on choosing π_β are absent

Critical missing ablations: no evaluation of necessity of negative examples (Section 3.6), no principled justification for block-wise aggregation design, and limited exploration of stabilization alternatives
Incomplete transferability validation: transfer tested only within same domain (logic puzzles); generalization to different domains unclear

Presentation issues: Section 2.2 relies on well-known distribution shift concepts without clearly delineating novel insights; Figure 1 is cluttered; novelty relative to Kang et al. (2025) is understated; claims appear cherry-picked (e.g., '14.6% gain' claim from Table 2 represents selective reporting)

strengths: Clear and important problem identification: demonstrates empirically that offline SFT performance does not correlate with post-RL performance, addressing a gap in current LLM post-training approaches (Figure 1)
Well-motivated approach grounded in off-policy evaluation (OPE) theory: clear connection between behavior policy (offline data) and target policy (online RL) mismatch with principled solutions

Strong and consistent empirical results: 40% absolute accuracy gain on logic games, up to 14.6% Pass@8 improvement on AIME-2025, consistent improvements across 6 models (0.6B-8B) and multiple benchmarks

Practical method with low implementation overhead: simple importance sampling-based reweighting compatible with both NLL and KL-based objectives; plug-in approach with minimal changes to existing pipelines
Comprehensive experimental breadth: multiple model families, task domains, evaluation metrics; controlled setup with synthetic games; good ablation studies (sequence/token/block variants)
Useful analysis and insights: Section 4.6 shows PEAR concentrates learning on important tokens, aligns offline/online gradients better, and reduces parameter drift (Figures 7-8)
Good intuitive presentation: Figure 2 and Section 2.2 provide clear motivation for the reweighting approach
weaknesses: Critical clarity issue on π_θ computation during training: when and how are target policy probabilities computed (at initialization, periodically, or online)? This affects both reproducibility and soundness but is underspecified in Section 3.2

No experimental comparison with concurrent related work: acknowledges multiple concurrent methods (iw-SFT, DFT, ASFT, Proximal-SFT, etc.) but provides no quantitative comparisons, making positioning in the literature unclear
Lack of statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, significance testing, or random seed reporting; single-run results make it unclear if improvements are meaningful vs. noise
Limited scope and generalization: all evaluations on verifiable reasoning tasks (logic games, math); no evidence the method works for language generation, alignment, or other post-training objectives
Incomplete baseline coverage in main results: Figure 1 shows many baselines but Table 2 focuses on basic SFT; why aren't stronger baselines (TopLogP, etc.) included in math benchmark results?
Method novelty is incremental: importance sampling for offline learning is established; connection to SFT is straightforward; core novelty is problem framing rather than technical innovation

Underspecified implementation details: claimed 'little' computational overhead but not measured; no code availability; how π_θ is computed during training is ambiguous; evaluation set handling unclear
Limited hyperparameter sensitivity analysis: γ=0.999 only; clip bounds and block size B variations shown but not systematically studied; no analysis of how often bounds are violated
Incomplete failure analysis: no discussion of when PEAR fails or underperforms; no analysis of task distributions where method degrades
Inconsistent Pass@1 vs Pass@K improvements: Table 2 shows strong Pass@8/64 gains but often minimal Pass@1 improvements (e.g., +1% Pass@1 vs +0% Pass@8 for 8B AIME25); pattern not explained
